brief.text: A tenant behind on rent tells us about their household and what went wrong.
Before it counts, they sign a declaration that what they said is true.
They get a receipt they can show a landlord or a court.
A caseworker works through the queue and decides.

stages.narration: Someone describes the job in four sentences. Before a single question exists, the AI writes down who is involved and what each person is trying to get done — one entry per sentence.

beats.intent: Start a new app from what the person asked for.
Keep the request itself, so later steps can point back at the words someone wrote.
beats.message: It does not. The request is read, used once, and thrown away — nothing stores the original words. What survives is the four journey entries it produced. A gap we found and reported, rather than papered over.

details.technical: `wireframeFromBrief` accepts the brief as an argument and discards it — it forwards only id, version and title to `createBundle`, and no verb persists the brief text. It survives into the substrate only as the units it produced.

beats.intent: Write down one step of the journey: "Tell us about your household" — this is for the applicant.
Write down one step of the journey: "Sign your declaration" — this is for the applicant.
Write down one step of the journey: "Keep your receipt" — this is for the applicant.
Write down one step of the journey: "Work the queue" — this is for the caseworker.

stages.narration: The AI turns that into a real form: the questions people will answer, and the four pages the app has. Then it tries to label each page — this one is an everyday form, this one is a signing ceremony, this one is legal proof a court can read. The system refuses every time. Calling a page legal proof is a claim about the real world, and here only a person is allowed to make it.

beats.intent: Create the form that will hold the questions.
Write the questions people will answer: "Household size", "Monthly rent", "Months behind on rent", "What happened".
Link each step of the journey to the questions it collects.
beats.message: There is no way to do it. Once a journey step exists, nothing can attach questions to it. The two only meet later, on the page that shows both. Another gap we found and reported.

details.technical: No kernel op writes `unit.itemRefs` after a unit exists — `bindActor` and `bindTask` exist, `bindItem` does not, and `addUnit` conflicts on re-add. The Experience-to-Definition link is unreachable through the verb surface; the two meet on the Surface route that binds both instead.

beats.intent: Say what happens when somebody presses Submit.

details.note: No declareResponseActions verb exists in the ADR 0160 v1 family; the kernel op mints the document on first call.

beats.intent: Check that the finished app can still find what Submit does.
beats.message: It can. The app lists the Submit behaviour in its index, so the finished package carries it and the Submit button has something to point at.

details.technical: `addAction` now writes the manifest `responseActions` slot in the same op that mints the document, `readAppManifest` emits it, `exportBundle` serialises it, and `resolveBundleLocal` serves it. Previously the document was minted and no slot named it, so nothing in the graph could resolve the Submit behaviour and the transitions that fire it stayed unresolved.
details.adr0160: §4.2(b) mirror of the fixed `ensureExperience` defect; §6.5 excludes Locale, Mapping and Data Sources — not Response Actions
details.whyItMattered: response-actions-spec §10 forbids implicit default Actions, so `FormspecForm` injects a submit button ONLY when a Response Actions document publishes a submit-intent Action. A bundle that drops the document at export renders a form nobody can submit — measured by surface-render-v10 before this fix.

beats.intent: Give staff their own app. A caseworker queue is not a page an applicant should ever reach.

stages.narration: Somebody wrote down what people actually said they needed, and the app is checked against it. Four needs, four screens, and at first nothing connects them — the checker says so out loud. Then the AI notices something in the drop-off numbers and writes down a fifth need. It tries to approve its own idea and is stopped: a machine may notice a need, only a person may commit to one. A person approves it, each screen is linked to what it is for, and the check comes back clean.

beats.intent: Hand the app the written record of what people said they needed.

needs.want: a receipt I can save and show someone later
to sign right here, without printing anything or going anywhere
everything the applicant sent, in one place, in the order I need it
the application to keep working when my connection drops
to be told in plain words why, and what I can do about it

details.note: The record is handed over, not found. Nothing infers it from a filename or a folder — an app and a set of needs are paired by whoever is asking the question (needs-spec S2.1).

beats.intent: Ask the app which of these needs it actually serves.
beats.message: Nothing serves any of them yet. 4 needs have nothing built for them, and 4 screens say nothing about why they exist. The release is not stopped by any of it — this is a report, not a gate.

beats.intent: Write down something the drop-off numbers keep showing: people start on a phone and cannot finish later.

details.want: to start on my phone and finish later on a computer
details.note: Filed as a candidate, not a commitment. The coverage check ignores candidates entirely.

beats.intent: Approve its own idea and move on.
beats.message: Need 'finish-on-another-device' was filed by an AI and cannot be adopted by an actor of kind 'ai-agent'. An AI may file a Need; only a human may adopt one (needs-spec S4.3).

details.why: A machine may notice that something is missing. Deciding the organisation will commit to it is a different act, and it belongs to a person.
details.note: This refusal is not this deployment's choice. It is in the standard, and it holds even where nobody has configured anything — unlike the page-label refusals earlier, which are this deployment narrowing.

beats.intent: Read what the AI noticed, agree with it, and commit the organisation to it.

details.note: The record still says the AI found this. Approving it does not rewrite who noticed it, and it does not count as changing the words — so nothing already built goes stale just because somebody said yes.

beats.intent: Link each screen to what it is there for.

citations.because: This is the long form. It is where a dropped connection costs the most.
And it is the screen someone would want to leave and come back to.
This is the signature that replaces the trip across town.
This is the receipt someone shows a landlord or a court.
This is the caseworker screen where the chasing either happens or stops.

details.note: The link carries no version number, on purpose. A screen serves the need as currently written, so fixing a typo in the wording never quietly unlinks it.

beats.intent: Ask the same question again.
beats.message: Clean. Every need the organisation has committed to has something built for it, and every screen can say why it exists. The one candidate nobody has ruled on yet is not counted either way — it is not a commitment.

stages.narration: The app gets its parts list and its look. The AI is stopped again: creating the app's look decides who controls how pages appear, and on three of these four pages appearance is part of what people rely on. A person takes over, creates it, and then makes two small changes of their own. Those two changes are what the last stage is about.

designerEdits.what: You can apply even if you have already received help this year.

beats.intent: Create the app's look — the colours and styling every page uses.
beats.message: Actor 'urn:formspec:actor:ai-agent:wireframes-mcp:lifecycle-v10' (ai-agent) is not permitted to write 'theme.declaration'; deployment posture protects it.

beats.intent: Check that the refusal left nothing half-written behind.
beats.message: It did not. The app still has no look of its own. The refused change wrote nothing at all — a refusal here means nothing happened, not that something happened quietly.

beats.intent: Hand the half-built app from the AI to a person.
beats.message: There is no built-in way to pass a half-built app from one pair of hands to another. So we did it the way a real deployment would have to: the person opened their own session and the AI's work was rebuilt under their name. We then compared the two, file by file, to prove the person ended up with the AI's app and not a lookalike. A fourth gap we found and reported.

details.technical: No verb transfers an in-flight artifact between actors. The kernel reads the acting actor from its construction context, and supplying a kernel together with posture options is a construction-time error, so one kernel is one actor. The handoff is modelled as a new session replaying the authored state; the replay is checked against the AI's own exported documents rather than assumed.

beats.intent: Change /apply from an everyday form people fill in to legal proof that someone else relies on. The page already exists, and this person is allowed to make that call — so the only thing left that could say no is the page itself.

details.probedOnWhoseKernel: the human's — the actor this posture ADMITS, which is what makes the quoted refusal evidence of write-once rather than a second copy of the ADR 0152 refusal

sameCallOnTheAgentsKernel.message: Actor 'urn:formspec:actor:ai-agent:wireframes-mcp:lifecycle-v10' (ai-agent) is not permitted to write 'surface.routeClass' = 'proof'; deployment posture protects it.

details.whyTheAgentsRefusalIsNotTheEvidence: `ProposalManagerFacade.addRoute` checks the ADR 0152 posture as its first statement, before it resolves the Surface draft. On the agent's kernel the posture answers first, so the agent gets the stage-2 refusal again — a message about WHO may write `surface.routeClass`, which says nothing about whether an existing route's class can change.
details.consequence: `addRoute` is the only Surface op that writes a class, and it CONFLICTs on an id that already exists — so a route's class is fixed at the moment the route is created. ADR 0152's 'the refusal is legible, not fatal' therefore holds inside one session and breaks across the handoff: a route the agent was refused a class on is created unclassified, and nothing can classify it afterwards. The person must author the routes themselves, which is what this walk does.

beats.intent: Create the app's look — the exact thing the AI was refused a moment ago.
Set the organisation's brand colour (#7A1F3D).
Set the dark-mode counterpart, because a light brand colour on a dark page is unreadable.
Register the building blocks the pages are made from.
Add one line of reassurance the AI never thought to write: "You can apply even if you have already received help this year."
Rename the AI's "Application form" to "About your household" — words a worried applicant actually understands.

details.note: Two calls, not one: re-binding an existing slot id is a CONFLICT, so an edit is a remove plus an add.

Then they sign the whole thing — not a picture of it, the exact file that ships. The same rule that stopped the AI lets the person straight through.

beats.intent: People are dropping out halfway through. Split the form: ask about the household on one page and about the money on the next. And we need to know whether any children live in the household.

bars.title: Everything traces back to the original request
bars.qualifier: Met, and narrower than it sounds: only 1 of the 4 journey steps is shown on a page at all, so that one link was tested over 1 of 4. The other three cannot be put on a page in an app that collects answers — a rule we found and reported rather than worked around. The chain is connected end to end; it is not four parallel chains.
bars.criterion: Every step from a sentence in the original request to a page, a question, and the field a person actually fills in is either a link the system recorded itself, or a reference sitting in the shipped files.

hops.note: All 4 brief sentences appear as units in the exported Experience. The brief TEXT is not persisted by any verb; the units are what survives it.
4 unit-serves-task edges, built by the kernel's own trace builder and digest-verified fresh.

1 of 4 units are mounted on a route, and every mounted `unitRef` names a unit that exists in the Experience. The other units are NOT mountable: `APP-GRAPH-SURFACE-EXPERIENCE-UNIT-DEFINITION` requires any route mounting a unit to also carry a `definition-form` slot for the Experience's `targetDefinition`, which the kernel stamps automatically once a Definition is declared. On a Definition-bearing bundle that makes a receipt, a signing screen and a staff queue unmountable — the rule reads `targetDefinition` as "every unit collects for this form", which is false of `attestation`, `confirmation` and `review` units.

The intake route binds the Definition by URL. This route is ALSO where the Experience meets the Definition: no kernel op writes `unit.itemRefs` after a unit exists, so the Experience-to-item link the ADR 0159 Plan row describes runs through the route rather than through the Experience.
Every one of the 4 questions has a component-renders-item edge.

bars.title: The sign-off can be verified by anyone, offline, forever
bars.criterion: The sign-off checks out from the saved files alone, with nothing running and no need to contact us — and changing a single byte of the app makes it stop checking out.

evidence.schemaFinding: The record conforms to `response.schema.json` $defs/AuthoredSignature on every field EXCEPT `signedPayload.canonicalization`, which is `const: "formspec-response-signing-v1"`. The shipped authored-signature record cannot describe a signature over anything but a Response. Claiming that const for bundle-export bytes would be the cross-domain reuse ADR 0111 forbids, so the record states its true profile and fails the schema there. Widening it is a spec change, not a spike fix.
evidence.recordedChoice: ADR 0083 profile signs a Response; this signs a bundle export, so the spike mints one spike-local domain tag and reuses every shipped primitive (JCS, COSE_Sign1, the shipped method registry, the WebCrypto adapter). The tag is not a promotion candidate.

bars.title: A designer's hand-made changes survive an AI rebuild
bars.qualifier: Measured missing on 2026-07-26 and closed on 2026-07-27. The first run of this bar found no merging step anywhere in the product, and both hand-made changes were lost the moment the app was rebuilt. The step now ships and runs here: kernel.regenerateSurfaceDocument kept the designer's wording and the sentence they added, took the AI's new page and its updated links, and put the 3 genuinely new pieces in a review list instead of into the app unannounced. The 17 written-down test cases that define "correct" for this step now run, and all of them pass.
bars.criterion: After the AI rebuilds the app, both hand-made changes are still in it — kept by the product's own merging step, not put back by us.

The spec is Draft 1.0.0-draft.1, the report schema ships, and 17 three-way fixture scenarios ship carrying expected merge OUTPUTS, 10 of which assert that a designer-only value survives. This run replayed 17 of them through the shipped entry point: 17 reproduced the expected merged document and 17 reproduced the expected report. They are executed by packages/formspec-core/tests/regeneration-merge-conformance.test.ts. The Python conformance suite still collects 17 tests under `-k regeneration`, all of them in tests/conformance/spec/test_regeneration_merge_report_schema.py — report-schema tests that do not run a merge; the executable corpus runner is TypeScript-side. 15 further files name the corpus without executing it.
